the-goddess-1934.gazette: Lianhua released The Goddess in 1934, when the Leftist Film Movement was pushing Shanghai's studios toward the city's tenements, pawnshops and night streets. The film puts a prostitute's earnings, a landlord, a school board and a neighborhood's opinion into the same ledger and lets the arithmetic run. Ruan Lingyu, who plays her, died the following March.

the-grapes-of-wrath-1940.gazette: The Farm Security Administration ran the migrant camps the film reconstructs, and FSA photographers were working the same highways while the picture was in production. Dust Bowl migration was not history in 1940; it was a live federal problem with a paper trail. Audiences could hold the screen against photographs printed that same year.

spellbound-1945.gazette: Selznick put his own analyst, May Romm, on the payroll as psychiatric adviser and her credit on the screen. In 1945 psychoanalysis was arriving in American popular life carrying the authority of medicine, and the production borrowed that authority in full. The therapy that reached audiences ran at the speed of a thriller: one buried scene, one afternoon, one cure.
spellbound-1945.prism: The credit is the load-bearing part. Once a practicing analyst's name is attached, the treatment stops being set dressing and becomes a claim about how minds get repaired — and 1945 clinical practice is on record to be checked against.

sunset-boulevard-1950.gazette: Erich von Stroheim plays a ruined director attending the star he once directed; he had in fact directed Gloria Swanson, and the footage Norma Desmond screens at home comes from their unfinished Queen Kelly. Cecil B. DeMille appears as himself, on the Paramount lot where he was actually shooting. Hollywood supplied the evidence for its own indictment.

the-wages-of-fear-1953.gazette: The tension is mechanical before it is dramatic: real trucks, real loads, real grades, built with practical effects rather than trickery, in southern France standing in for Latin America. Clouzot's shoot ran long and rough, and the difficulty stayed visible in the frame. Seven decades on, the discourse around the film is still largely about how it was physically done.

night-and-fog-1956.gazette: The archive came first — liberation footage, camp photographs, German records — and Resnais cut it against color material shot at Auschwitz-Birkenau ten years after the war. The commentary was written by Jean Cayrol, who had been deported to Mauthausen. French censors took issue with a single image: a French gendarme standing guard at a transit camp.
night-and-fog-1956.prism: The censors' objection is the tell. A record that indicts only the enemy is easy to publish; the frame they wanted removed was the one placing a French uniform inside the machinery.

12-angry-men-1957.gazette: Reginald Rose wrote the script after serving on a New York jury, and lawyers have been arguing with it ever since. The film's most celebrated turn — a juror producing a duplicate knife he bought near the crime scene — is misconduct under the rules that govern actual deliberation. Its authority and its central irregularity are the same scene.

fires-on-the-plain-1959.gazette: The source was a soldier's own war: Ooka Shohei served in the Philippines and was taken prisoner there, and wrote the Leyte collapse from close range. Starvation rations, units dissolving into the hills, and cannibalism among Japanese troops appear in the postwar record as well as in the novel. Ichikawa filmed it in 1959, for an audience that had supplied the soldiers.

the-400-blows-1959.gazette: No sets: Truffaut shot in working Paris apartments, classrooms and streets, and left the boy's session with the psychologist largely improvised. The observation center Antoine is sent to has a counterpart in Truffaut's own childhood — he was placed in one as a boy. The naturalism is the contract, and the camera keeps to it all the way to the beach.
the-400-blows-1959.prism: Naturalism here doubles as a defense — the more the camera behaves like a witness, the harder it is to file the neglect on screen under plot. The cost is that a childhood has to serve as evidence.

mughal-e-azam-1960.gazette: Akbar and Prince Salim are in the Mughal record; Anarkali largely is not, surviving in travelers' tales rather than court chronicles. K. Asif's production stretched across years and spent its resources on scale, building a court whose splendor is itself the argument. Indian critics have been separating the documented from the legendary in it ever since.

the-cloud-capped-star-1960.gazette: Ritwik Ghatak came out of East Bengal after Partition, and the refugee colony on the edge of Calcutta was a place he had lived rather than researched. By 1960 those settlements were more than a decade old and still administered as temporary. The film keeps its accounts at household scale: one wage, one sacrificed daughter, one diagnosis.

chronicle-of-a-summer-1961.gazette: In the summer of 1960, an ethnographer and a sociologist carried new lightweight sync-sound equipment onto Paris streets and recorded strangers talking about their own lives. Rouch and Morin then screened the footage back to the people in it and filmed the reaction, objections included. The picture closes with the two filmmakers unable to agree on what they had captured.
chronicle-of-a-summer-1961.prism: Screening the rushes to the subjects doesn't neutralize the camera; it relocates the editing argument inside the film. Vérité's honesty is procedural — it exhibits the mediation instead of hiding it.

divorce-italian-style-1961.gazette: Article 587 of the Italian penal code reduced the punishment for a man who killed a wife caught in adultery, and divorce was not legal in Italy at all. Germi's comedy runs on the collision of those two facts: murder was the cheaper exit from a marriage. The article stayed in force until 1981.

cleo-from-5-to-7-1962.gazette: Varda ran a clock. The chapters are timestamped and the running time tracks the fiction almost minute for minute, from five in the afternoon toward half past six, most of it shot on working Paris streets. A taxi radio carries dispatches from Algeria; the war was current, and the soundtrack simply lets it in.

lawrence-of-arabia-1962.gazette: Seven Pillars of Wisdom was already on the shelf, along with the Arab Revolt's official paperwork; Lean's film works from that record and bends it. Officers and Arab commanders are compressed into composites, and a campaign of years is fitted to an evening. T. E. Lawrence's surviving brother publicly repudiated the portrait.
lawrence-of-arabia-1962.prism: A subject who already authored his own legend makes a strange source: Lean is bending a document that was bent to begin with. The film's version won anyway, which is what tends to happen when the picture is better lit than the archive.
